rows.citation: Ezio Bartocci, Leonardo Mariani, Dejan Nickovic, et al. (2025). Signal Feature Coverage and Testing for CPS Dataflow Models. ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology, 34(7), Article 199, 1-37.
rows.model_type: Simulink dataflow models of cyber-physical systems (five models tested against ten Signal Temporal Logic properties)
rows.controlled_mutations: yes - FIM fault-injection tool with seven Simulink operators (noise, bias, negate, ROR, S2P, P2S, ASR); first-order mutants used to score test suites.
rows.multiple_stimuli: yes - many input-signal test cases generated per model by particle-swarm search; generated test inputs, not a fixed library of named protocols.
rows.electrophysiology_features: partial - ten generic signal features (mean, SD, RMS, shape factor, skewness, kurtosis, peak, impulse/crest factor, instantaneous frequency); not electrophysiological.
rows.protocol_optimization: partial - search-based test generation maximising signal-feature coverage within a time budget; not selection of a compact battery from a mutant-detection matrix.
rows.heldout_evaluation: no - mutants only evaluate generated suites (coverage is not tuned on mutants); no discovery/held-out split of models or fault families described.
rows.ai_transformations: no - faults are tool-injected mutants; no AI-assisted model edits studied.
rows.software: fct_master data package, https://gitlab.com/DrishtiYadav/fct_master (license reported as MIT by GitLab API)
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Structurally closest in this batch (signal features plus mutation scoring) but for CPS Simulink test generation. NeuroSem would use eFEL electrophysiology features, rheobase-normalised current-clamp protocols, refinement-calibrated tolerances, greedy selection on discovery mutants, held-out models and a held-out mutation family, and valid-transformation false-positive controls.
rows.verification_method: Crossref works API (10.1145/3714467: title, authors, vol 34 issue 7, pp 1-37); OpenAlex abstract; open-access version-of-record PDF from BOA Milano-Bicocca (boa.unimib.it/handle/10281/591661) read with pypdf (sections 3-4, Table 5); GitLab API for the repository.
rows.found_via: WebSearch site:dl.acm.org test selection simulation models cyber-physical Simulink mutation; verified via Crossref

rows.citation: Aitor Arrieta, Shuai Wang, Urtzi Markiegi, et al. (2019). Pareto efficient multi-objective black-box test case selection for simulation-based testing. Information and Software Technology, 114, 137-154.
rows.model_type: Simulink simulation models of cyber-physical systems (six case studies, one industrial)
rows.controlled_mutations: partial - Simulink mutants from previously published operators used only to measure fault revelation; undetected, duplicate and always-killed mutants filtered out.
rows.multiple_stimuli: yes - existing suites of 120-150 input-signal test cases per model form the pool that selection draws from.
rows.electrophysiology_features: partial - black-box output measures (anti-patterns such as instability, discontinuity, growth; input/output similarity); not electrophysiological features.
rows.protocol_optimization: yes - NSGA-II (plus NSGA-III, MOEA/D) selects test subsets trading six effectiveness measures against simulation-time cost; compared with random search and white-box coverage.
rows.heldout_evaluation: partial - selection objectives do not use mutants, so mutation score is an independent check; no held-out models or fault families.
rows.ai_transformations: no - no AI-generated or AI-assisted model changes.
rows.software: IST2019Paper replication material, https://github.com/aitorarrietamarcos/IST2019Paper (no license detected by GitHub API)
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Anticipates the runtime-cost framing of test selection for expensive simulations, validated with mutants. NeuroSem differs by selecting directly on a discovery mutant-by-protocol detection matrix, using neuroscience stimulation protocols and eFEL features with calibrated tolerances, and testing generalisation to held-out models and a held-out mutation family.
rows.verification_method: Crossref works API (authors, vol 114, pp 137-154); Semantic Scholar Graph API abstract; green open-access author manuscript PDF (ebiltegia.mondragon.edu) read with pypdf (sections 2, 4.2-4.3, Table 2); GitHub REST API for the repository.
rows.found_via: OpenAlex search 'mutation analysis Simulink test selection'; verified via Crossref

rows.citation: Seema Jehan, Franz Wotawa (2023). An Empirical Study of Greedy Test Suite Minimization Techniques Using Mutation Coverage. IEEE Access, 11, 65427-65442.
rows.model_type: general software (JavaScript NPM packages with their accompanying test suites)
rows.controlled_mutations: yes - Mutode tool (48 operators) generates mutants of NPM packages; a mutation matrix records which tests kill which mutants.
rows.multiple_stimuli: no - selection units are unit tests of JavaScript packages, not stimulation protocols applied to a dynamical model.
rows.electrophysiology_features: no - uses mutant kill outcomes and mutation score; no signal or feature extraction.
rows.protocol_optimization: yes - compares Greedy, DelayedGreedy, Harrold et al., LinMIN and DeltaMIN minimisation on mutation coverage; parameter alpha allows a small mutation-score loss.
rows.heldout_evaluation: no - reduction and fault-detection loss are judged on the same mutation score used for minimisation; no held-out programs or mutant families found.
rows.ai_transformations: no - no AI-assisted code changes studied.
rows.software: none verified (paper states artifacts are on GitHub, its reference [54]; URL not retrieved - unverified)
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Confirms that greedy set-cover minimisation over mutant kills is established, so NeuroSem's selection step alone is not novel. NeuroSem would differ by applying it to stimulation protocols with feature-level tolerances, adding count- and runtime-matched random baselines, and evaluating on held-out models and a held-out mutation family.
rows.verification_method: Crossref works API (vol 11, pp 65427-65442); OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar abstracts; full-text HTML retrieved from the IEEE Xplore REST endpoint (ieeexplore.ieee.org/rest/document/10160008) - the PDF link returned HTTP 418/HTML shell and the DOAJ page returned 403.

rows.citation: Frank T. Bergmann, Herbert M. Sauro (2008). Comparing simulation results of SBML capable simulators. Bioinformatics, 24(17), 1963-1965.
rows.model_type: biochemical reaction-network ODE models in SBML (150 curated BioModels Database models) run on several deterministic simulators
rows.controlled_mutations: no - unmodified curated models; divergences come from simulator differences, not injected faults.
rows.multiple_stimuli: no - one fixed time-course run per model (0-10 s, 1000 output points); no input protocols varied.
rows.electrophysiology_features: no - compares state-variable trajectories using pairwise relative errors and an agreement metric; no feature extraction.
rows.protocol_optimization: no - no selection or optimisation of test conditions.
rows.heldout_evaluation: no - descriptive cross-simulator comparison without any selection or data split.
rows.software: SBW-based comparison command-line tools and viewer, http://sys-bio.org/sbwWiki/compare (as stated in paper; current availability unverified)
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Systems-biology precedent for detecting simulator-induced divergence on standard-format models by comparing trajectories. NeuroSem would add controlled single-fault mutants and valid transformations, multiple current-clamp protocols, electrophysiology features with refinement-calibrated tolerances, compact battery selection, and held-out evaluation.
rows.verification_method: Crossref works API (vol 24 issue 17, pp 1963-1965); OpenAlex abstract; Europe PMC search (PMID 18579569, PMC2732216; fullTextXML returned empty); publisher PDF via academic.oup.com read with pypdf (Methods and Results).
rows.found_via: WebSearch site:dl.acm.org testing ODE simulators systems biology SBML (cited in snippet); verified via Crossref

rows.citation: R. J. Flassig, K. Sundmacher (2012). Optimal design of stimulus experiments for robust discrimination of biochemical reaction networks. Bioinformatics, 28(23), 3089-3096.
rows.model_type: nonlinear ODE biochemical reaction-network models (MAPK cascade with alternative feedbacks; Schloegl model)
rows.controlled_mutations: partial - discriminates hypothesised alternative model structures (e.g. two negative-feedback variants), not systematically generated single-fault mutants.
rows.multiple_stimuli: partial - optimises a time-varying input stimulus via control-vector parameterisation; the output is a designed stimulus, not a battery of protocols.
rows.electrophysiology_features: no - compares model response probability distributions via model overlap (expected likelihood); no interpretable feature extraction.
rows.protocol_optimization: yes - optimal-control design of stimuli maximising robust model discrimination under parameter uncertainty using sigma-point propagation.
rows.heldout_evaluation: partial - designs checked against Monte Carlo sampling of parameter distributions; no held-out models or model families.
rows.software: MATLAB/AMPL implementation, http://www.uni-magdeburg.de/ivt/svt/person/rf/roed.html (as stated in paper; current availability unverified)
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Model-based optimal experimental design for telling apart a few candidate structures via a continuous stimulus. NeuroSem would instead select discrete, interpretable current-clamp protocols by empirical detection coverage over many single-fault mutants, with feature tolerances, random cost-matched baselines and held-out generalisation.
rows.verification_method: Crossref works API (vol 28 issue 23, pp 3089-3096); OpenAlex abstract; Europe PMC full-text XML (PMC3516143, PMID 23047554); publisher article page academic.oup.com.
rows.found_via: WebSearch site:ieeexplore.ieee.org optimal stimulus design discriminate neuron models experimental design (PMC link); verified via Crossref

rows.citation: Frankie Patten-Elliott, Chon Lok Lei, Simon P. Preston, et al. (2024). Optimising experimental designs for model selection of ion channel drug binding mechanisms. bioRxiv (preprint).
rows.model_type: cardiac hERG ion-channel ODE models combined with 15 candidate drug-binding mechanism models (voltage clamp)
rows.controlled_mutations: partial - 15 alternative drug-binding mechanism models act as competing variants; not single recorded faults applied to one reference model.
rows.multiple_stimuli: partial - voltage-clamp protocols parameterised by six step voltages and two durations; optimised designs compared with a simple previously used protocol.
rows.electrophysiology_features: no - compares simulated current outputs and log-likelihood fits; no eFEL-style features, and voltage rather than current clamp.
rows.protocol_optimization: yes - CMA-ES maximises the median pairwise squared output difference between fitted candidate models to improve model selection.
rows.heldout_evaluation: partial - robustness examined with a different data-generating hERG model (model discrepancy case); no held-out model or variant families.
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Optimising protocols to separate ion-channel model variants parallels choosing stimuli that expose model differences. NeuroSem differs in setting (neuron current clamp), goal (regression detection after edits rather than mechanism selection), discrete greedy battery selection on mutants, feature tolerances, cost-matched random baselines, and held-out models and mutation family.
rows.verification_method: Crossref works API (posted-content, five authors); bioRxiv API (v1 posted 2024-08-21, cc_by, no published version found); OpenAlex; full text at biorxiv.org (methods on protocol parameterisation, objective, evaluation); GitHub REST API for repository and license.
